opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way we think about it is that the decoder isn't just a sequence of kernels you launch one at a time. It's really a dataflow graph, and the whole point of a reconfigurable dataflow architecture is that you can lay that graph out spatially in hardware rather than time-multiplexing it through a fixed pipeline the way you would on a GPU.

So when you have a large model, say a big decoder-only transformer, the first question is how you partition it across the 16 RDUs. You've got a couple of dimensions to play with. You can do tensor parallelism, where you split the individual matrix multiplies, the attention heads and the MLP weights, across chips. You can also do pipeline-style partitioning, where different layers live on different chips. In practice you want a combination, and the compiler is the thing that figures out the right balance, because what you're really optimizing for is keeping the data on chip and moving as little as possible across the chip-to-chip links.

The key idea for us is what we call operator fusion at a very aggressive level. On a GPU, each operator, whether it's a layer norm, a matmul, a softmax, or a rotary embedding, tends to be its own kernel. You write results back out to HBM and then read them back in for the next kernel. That's a lot of memory traffic, and for decoding, where you're generating one token at a time and the batch is small, you're completely memory-bandwidth bound. With the RDU, we can take an entire decoder layer, or even multiple layers, and map them onto the compute and memory units on the chip as one fused dataflow pipeline. The activations stream from one stage to the next through on-chip SRAM and never go back out to off-chip memory.

Then the memory hierarchy matters a lot. We have a three-tier memory system: the on-chip SRAM, high-bandwidth memory, and then a large DDR capacity tier. That lets you hold the weights of very big models, or many models at once, and stage them into HBM and then onto the chip as needed. When you spread a decoder across 16 RDUs, you're essentially aggregating the HBM bandwidth of all 16 chips, and since token generation is bandwidth bound, that aggregate bandwidth is what translates directly into tokens per second.

So the mental model is: fuse as much as you can so you stay on chip, partition across chips so you can use all the memory bandwidth in parallel, and minimize communication at the boundaries. When you get that right, you can get really high single-user token throughput for inference, which is exactly what you want for things like agentic workloads where you're chaining lots of model calls together and latency compounds.

r001.rationale: The response describes aggressive operator fusion and mapping an entire decoder layer or multiple layers as a fused dataflow pipeline, but it does not state that the whole decoder is combined into a single kernel as compiler fusion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way we think about it starts from the dataflow idea itself. If you look at a decoder block, it's really a graph of operators: you've got the attention projections, the softmax, the feed-forward layers, the normalizations, and all the data movement between them. On a GPU, you execute that graph one kernel at a time, and between every kernel you're going out to memory and coming back. With the RDU, what we do is take that whole graph and spatially lay it out across the chip, so the output of one operator flows directly into the next without touching off-chip memory. That's the fundamental win, and it's what the compiler is built around.

Now, when you talk about 16 RDUs, the question becomes how you partition that graph. There are really two dimensions. One is the familiar tensor-parallel or pipeline-parallel partitioning that people do today across GPUs, where you split layers or split the matrices within a layer. But the other dimension, which is more unique to us, is that we have a lot of on-chip SRAM, hundreds of megabytes per device, and we can use that to hold the weights of a set of layers resident. So the way you'd map a model like a Llama 3 70B, for example, is you spread the layers across the 16 devices so that the entire set of weights fits in aggregate on-chip memory, and then tokens stream through the system in a pipelined fashion. Each device is responsible for some set of layers, it holds those weights locally, and the activations are what move between chips.

The important thing is that the compiler is making those decisions, not the programmer. The user gives us a PyTorch model, the compiler lowers it into a dataflow graph, and then it has a cost model that reasons about on-chip memory capacity, compute balance, and the bandwidth between devices, and it searches for a mapping that keeps everything on-chip and keeps the pipeline balanced. You don't want one device sitting idle because it got a lighter set of layers. And for the decode phase, which is memory-bandwidth-bound on a GPU because you're reading all the weights for every single token, having the weights in SRAM means we can generate tokens at a rate that's really just limited by how fast we can move activations through the pipeline. That's where the big speedups come from.

The other thing I'd say is that this isn't a one-off exercise. We also have the three-tier memory system, with the SRAM, the HBM, and then DDR, so you can hold many models resident and switch between them quickly. So the mapping question isn't just "how do I lay out one decoder," it's "how do I lay out a decoder so that I can also hold ten others and swap in microseconds." That changes how you think about the problem versus just a single-model deployment.

r001.rationale: The response says the compiler spatially lays out the decoder graph so operators pass data directly, but it does not identify combining the whole decoder into a single kernel as compiler fusion.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is to start with the dataflow graph of the decoder: what are the operations, and how does data move between them? Then you partition that graph across the 16 RDUs, taking into account both the computation and where the weights and intermediate results need to live.

You can put successive layers on different RDUs and pipeline the work through them, or you can spread an individual layer across multiple RDUs. The right balance depends on the size of the model and whether you’re optimizing for latency or throughput. If you just divide the operations evenly but create a lot of communication, you haven’t necessarily made it faster.

So the goal is to keep the data close to the computation, balance the work, and have the compiler orchestrate that movement. You want to think of those 16 RDUs as one system executing the decoder, rather than as 16 independent devices.

r001.rationale: The response discusses partitioning the decoder graph across RDUs and compiler orchestration, but does not identify combining the whole decoder into a single kernel as compiler fusion.

sol-6.1.text:
The way to think about it is that you’re mapping a computation graph onto a set of resources. A decoder has these different operations—attention, matrix multiplications, feed-forward layers—and the question is how to partition those operations across the 16 RDUs, while also deciding where the weights and intermediate results live.

You could put successive parts of the decoder on different RDUs and pipeline the computation through them. You can also split a large operation across multiple RDUs. So you’re combining pipeline parallelism with parallelism within an operation. The compiler’s job is to find a mapping that balances the work and keeps data moving efficiently, because you don’t want one RDU doing all the work while the others are waiting, or communication dominating the computation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses partitioning decoder operations across RDUs and pipelining or splitting them, but does not identify combining the whole decoder into a single kernel as compiler fusion.
